research_phase.full_response:
Yes. Let  $n=|V(G)|$ ,  $d=|S|-\beta_2(G)$ , and  $A=\Delta-1$ . The aggregate cut proves
$$\boxed{\displaystyle d\le
\left\lfloor\frac{An}{12A+4\delta-6}\right\rfloor.}$$
For  $\delta\ge3$ , the unrounded inequality is strict. In particular, for integer degree bounds,
$$\boxed{\displaystyle d\le
\left\lfloor\frac{An-1}{12A+4\delta-6}\right\rfloor.}$$
The obstruction to equality comes from the selected leaves. Equality would require  $2c$  leaves to have neighbours in  $U$ , with each vertex of  $U$  serving exactly one leaf, yet it would force  $|U|<2c$ .1. The chosen witnesses and the single cutWrite  $C,L,I,P$  for the selected star centres, their leaves, selected isolates, and selected edge-component vertices. Put  $c=|C|$ ,  $e=|L|=2c+s$ , and  $m=|P|$ . A selected vertex is active if it has a selected neighbour. An outside vertex is formed precisely when it has at least two selected neighbours or has a single active selected neighbour. This criterion allows the forming star to be non-induced.Deleting a leaf  $\ell$  leaves its centre active, and the newly omitted  $\ell$  is formed by that centre and another leaf. Minimality therefore supplies an originally outside vertex that loses formation. Its selected neighbourhood is  $\{\ell\}$  or  $\{\ell,i\}$  for a selected isolate  $i$ . Indeed, no surviving selected vertex loses activity in this deletion.Call a centre clean if one of its leaves has a witness with selected neighbourhood exactly that leaf, and let  $q$  count the other centres. When a centre  $v$  is deleted, two of its leaves form the newly omitted  $v$ . An outside vertex losing formation without being adjacent to  $v$  must have had a unique selected neighbour that became inactive, hence a leaf of  $v$ . This would make  $v$  clean. Thus each of the  $q$  remaining centres has an adjacent deletion witness. Its selected neighbourhood is  $\{v\}$  or  $\{v,i\}$  for a selected isolate  $i$ . In the two-neighbour case the surviving neighbour is inactive after deletion, and bipartiteness prevents it from being a leaf of  $v$ , since that would give a triangle.Fix any permitted  $W$ . Choose one witness per leaf, using a private witness at one leaf of each clean centre, and one direct witness for each of the  $q$  other centres. Every chosen witness has a unique active selected owner, and these owners are distinct. In particular,
$$|W|=e+q,\qquad \boxed{|E(C,W)|=q}.$$
Each leaf witness contributes zero to the second count, and each direct witness contributes exactly one.Let  $U=V(G)\setminus(S\cup W)$ ,  $u=|U|$ , and  $h(i)=|N(i)\cap W|$  for  $i\in I$ . Write  $z_0,a,b_2,b_3$  for the counts with  $h=0,1,2,\ge3$ , respectively, and put  $t=a+b_2+b_3$ . Let  $I_0,I_1,I_+$  denote the isolates with  $h=0,1,>0$ . As in the free-unused exchange, put
$$Z=\{v\in U:N(v)\cap S\subseteq C\cup I_+\},\qquad g=|Z|.$$
The centres have exactly  $2c+s$  incidences inside  $S$  and exactly  $q$  into  $W$ . The  $a$  isolates of  $I_1$  have none inside  $S$  and exactly  $a$  into  $W$ . Adding their degree demands gives
$$(\delta-2)c+(\delta-1)a-s-q
\ \le\ |E(C\cup I_1,U)|
\ \le\ \Delta g+(\Delta-1)(u-g)=Au+g. \tag{1}$$
For the upper bound, each  $v\in U\setminus Z$  has a neighbour in  $L\cup P\cup I_0$ , disjoint from  $C\cup I_1$ . It therefore has at most  $\Delta-1$  neighbours in the union  $C\cup I_1$ . Each  $v\in Z$  has at most  $\Delta$  there. This counts the available capacity at each unused vertex once.2. The exchange and matching countsFor this same  $W$ , let  $\mu$  be the matching number in the supplied centre–helper multigraph. Its edges are the leaf witnesses touching an  $h=2$  isolate, joining the leaf’s centre to that isolate. Put  $H=b_3+\mu$ . The fixed counts give
$$\begin{aligned}
J&=c+s+2q-t-b_2-2b_3\ge0,\\
R&=c-q+b_2+b_3-\mu\ge2d,\\
2b_2&\le s+q+2\mu,\\
T'&=t-s-q\ge2d+g. \tag{2}
\end{aligned}$$
Here are the counting reasons. At least  $c-q$  chosen witnesses have no helper, and every other chosen witness has at most one. Hence  $t+b_2+2b_3\le |W|-(c-q)=c+s+2q$ , giving  $J\ge0$ .For  $R$ , take all of  $S\cup W$  of one colour, together with the opposite-colour selected edge vertices and isolates of  $h\le1$ . This is a dissociation set. In each colour construction, a matched centre of the retained colour gains one vertex by removing the matched leaf witness and adding its leaf and its  $h=2$  helper. The added leaf sees only its centre, and the helper sees only its other chosen witness. Distinct matching edges use distinct centres and helpers, and every witness has at most one helper, so the repairs coexist. The two colour constructions have total size  $2|S|-(c-q)-b_2-b_3+\mu$  after repair, proving  $R\ge2d$ . Also, of the  $2b_2$  witness incidences at twice-touched isolates, at most  $q$  come from direct witnesses. Keeping two leaves per centre discards at most  $s$  further incidences. The remaining bipartite multigraph has maximum degree two, so alternating edges on its paths and even cycles give  $2\mu\ge2b_2-q-s$ .For  $T'$ , retain  $S\setminus C$ , add the witnesses of one colour, remove the isolates they touch, and add  $Z$  of that same colour. Each retained leaf sees at most its own witness. Each added vertex of  $Z$  is isolated in the resulting set, since its selected neighbours are removed centres or touched isolates of the opposite colour. The two dissociation sets have total size  $2|S|+s+q-t+g$ , giving the last line of (2).Two consequences we need are
$$\begin{aligned}
2c&=J+R+T'+H\ge4d+g+H,\\
a&=T'+s+q-b_2-b_3
   \ge 2d+g+\frac{s+q}{2}-H. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}$$
The exact vertex count  $n=5c+2s+q+t+m+z_0+u$  also gives
$$n=\frac52J+\frac52R+\frac72T'+\frac52H+3s+2q+m+z_0+u.$$
Thus, writing  $\eta=n-12d$ ,
$$\eta\ge u+\frac72g+\frac52H+3s+2q+m+z_0. \tag{4}$$
3. Coefficient and quantified remainderSubstitute the two lower bounds (3) into the demand side of (1). Their multipliers  $\delta-2$  and  $\delta-1$  are nonnegative throughout the stated range. Collecting terms gives
$$(4\delta-6)d
\le Au+\frac{\delta}{2}H
-\frac{\delta-3}{2}(s+q)-\frac32(\delta-2)g. \tag{5}$$
Subtracting (5) from  $A$  times (4) yields the quantified remainder
$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}
An-(12A+4\delta-6)d\ \ge{}&
\frac{7A+3(\delta-2)}2\,g
+\frac{5A-\delta}{2}\,H\\
&+\left(3A+\frac{\delta-3}{2}\right)s
+\left(2A+\frac{\delta-3}{2}\right)q
+A(m+z_0).
\end{aligned}} \tag{6}$$
Every coefficient on the right is strictly positive for  $A\ge\delta-1\ge1$ .In particular, at  $\delta=2$  the right side of (5) contains  $+(s+q)/2$ . Retaining that term gives coefficients  $3A-\tfrac12$  and  $2A-\tfrac12$  for  $s,q$  in (6), both positive. The resulting bound is  $d\le\lfloor An/(12A+2)\rfloor$ . For all  $\delta\ge2$ , (6) and integrality of  $d$  prove the claimed floor bound.4. Why positive equality is impossible at  $\delta\ge3$ Suppose  $An=(12A+4\delta-6)d$ . Since  $G$  is nonempty,  $d>0$ . Equation (6) forces
$$g=H=s=q=m=z_0=0.$$
Then  $b_3=\mu=0$ , and (2) forces  $b_2=0$ . Equality must also hold in (4). Its exact vertex-count expansion consequently gives  $J=0$  and  $R=T'=2d$ . Hence
$$c=a=t=2d>0,\qquad e=2c .$$
Equality in (1) now gives
$$Au=(2\delta-3)c.$$
Every vertex of  $U$  is nonfree and saturates its capacity of  $A=\Delta-1$  neighbours in  $C\cup I_1$ . Its one remaining neighbour must lie in  $L\cup P\cup I_0=L$ . Therefore  $|E(L,U)|=u$ .Each of the  $2c$  leaves, in turn, has exactly two neighbours in  $S\cup W$ , its centre and its own chosen witness. At  $\delta\ge3$  each needs at least one neighbour in  $U$ , so  $u\ge2c$ . But saturation gives
$$u=\frac{2\delta-3}{A}c
\le\frac{2\delta-3}{\delta-1}c
=\left(2-\frac1{\delta-1}\right)c<2c.$$
This contradiction proves strictness. For integer  $\delta,\Delta$ , the slack  $An-(12A+4\delta-6)d$  is therefore at least one, giving the stated integer refinement.
